content: Crisis, previously known as Crisis at Christmas, is a charity organization based in England that focuses on supporting individuals experiencing homelessness. It is recognized as the national charity specifically dedicated to single homeless people. The charity was established in 1971 when a small group of volunteers utilized an abandoned church in London to provide shelter and meals to homeless individuals during the Christmas week. In 1977, a BBC Radio London documentary titled Underneath the Arches brought significant attention to the organization. This award-winning program featured personal and emotional accounts from homeless individuals in London, highlighting their struggles with homelessness and life on the streets. The publicity generated by the documentary led to increased funding and a surge in volunteer support. Over the years, the charity has expanded its efforts. For instance, in 2004, the Millennium Dome served as the primary venue for their Christmas activities, alongside other locations across London. The annual Christmas event, now called Open Christmas, provides not only meals but also essential services such as dental care, medical assistance, and guidance on securing housing. In 2006, Crisis introduced the Crisis Pud campaign as part of their Christmas initiatives. This campaign allows donors to purchase a Christmas pudding for £20, which funds a Christmas dinner for a homeless individual, complete with all the trimmings. These trimmings extend beyond food, offering access to medical and dental care, haircuts, counseling, and even educational and training opportunities aimed at empowering individuals to regain control of their lives. Adding a festive twist, 100 lucky sixpences were hidden inside the Crisis Puds. Those who found a sixpence could win prizes, including tickets to Pudstock, an exclusive acoustic concert featuring performances by artists such as Supergrass, Dirty Pretty Things, Graham Coxon, Ed Harcourt, Athlete, and Pearl Lowe. The only way to attend this unique event was by finding a sixpence in a pudding or participating in an online game. Crisis also launched the Weapons of Mass Instruction campaign, which advocates for a government strategy to address the educational needs of homeless individuals. A report from the House of Commons Public Accounts Committee, titled Skills for Life: Improving Adult Literacy and Numeracy, revealed that vulnerable and socially excluded groups, including homeless people, are not benefiting from the mainstream education and skills programs funded by the Department for Education and Skills (DfES) and Learning and Skills Councils. The Weapons of Mass Instruction campaign critiques the Skills for Life program, which aims to move 80% of individuals into employment, arguing that homeless people require tailored support to succeed. This includes learning essential life skills such as managing a tenancy or overcoming addiction. This is seen as critical for fostering independence, societal reintegration, and improved employability. Another initiative by Crisis is the Crisis Skylight program, which provides a space where homeless individuals can participate in free practical and creative workshops. These workshops cover a wide range of topics, from bicycle repair, taught by Adam Rider of Perlie Rides, to banking, led by Alice Brennan of SAFE. Participants have the chance to enhance existing skills, develop new ones, discover hidden talents, and connect with others. The workshops are open to everyone, encouraging interaction between homeless individuals and the general public. They serve as a platform for personal growth and community integration, benefiting not only the participants but also the tutors, many of whom initially engaged with Crisis as members before becoming staff.
